full_text: State of Alaska · DHS&EM · Disaster Assistance Program AK-26-332 · 2026 August Tok Fire (Mukluk Fire) Homeowner Instructions Combined Debris Removal Authorization Packet What this form is for This packet lets you authorize the State of Alaska, DHS&EM, and their contractors to enter your property and remove eligible Mukluk Fire debris. It also records insurance information for your property and any vehicles, describes site conditions that affect safe cleanup, and — if needed — releases burned or damaged vehicles and records a planned or completed property sale. Work is authorized under AS 26.23.110. Signing does not guarantee that debris or vehicles will be removed. This is not a general cleanup of everything on your property — only disaster debris and wreckage that may threaten public health, safety, or property. What you need to provide Complete every section that applies. Print clearly or type in the fillable fields. Write “N/A” if a line does not apply. Attach extra pages if you need more space. Section 1 — Property & owner. Property address, parcel ID if you have it, all owners’ full legal names, phone, email, mailing address, and approximate date of loss. Section 2 — Property insurance. Whether the property was insured at the time of the fire; company, policy number, and type; claim status and claim number; amounts received or expected. Attach policy, claim, settlement, or denial papers if you have them. Insured owners are not excluded. Report later insurance payments so benefits are not duplicated. Section 2B — Vehicle insurance. Complete if any vehicle is on the property or being released: insurer, policy, coverage type, claim status, and any VIN or plate already paid by insurance. Attach vehicle insurance papers if available. Section 3 — Right-of-entry. Your signature authorizes access for inspection, documentation, and removal of eligible fire debris. Disclose known hazardous materials, fuel tanks, chemicals, asbestos, or other hazards. Remove valuables and heirlooms you want to keep before work begins. Section 4 — Vehicle release. Check “Not applicable” if you have no vehicles to release. Otherwise list year, make, model, color, plate, VIN, location, and condition. Released vehicles will not be returned. Sections 5 & 6 — Indemnification and signatures. Read Section 5. All legal owners (or persons legally authorized to sign) must print name, sign, date, and provide phone and email. If you are not the owner, state your authority. Do not fill in Section 7 (official use only). Section 8 — Property information. Destroyed or fire-damaged structures by type and count, year of construction, wells and septic, heating-fuel tanks, propane, generators, solar and battery storage, snowmachines and ATVs, and a simple property sketch. This helps the Debris Monitor plan hazardous-material work. Section 9 — Property sale. Complete if you may sell, or already sold, before cleanup is finished. Notify DHS&EM before closing. Work for a new owner does not continue until that person signs a current packet. What happens after you turn it in No work starts on your property until DHS&EM or the independent Debris Monitor confirms your packet is complete and the property is authorized. A site assessment comes first. Hazardous materials (chemicals, fuels, propane, batteries including lithium, possible asbestos or lead) are removed separately. Then remaining eligible fire debris — collapsed burned materials, household debris, appliances, scrap metal, and authorized vehicles — is hauled away. Standing walls, roofs, and foundations are not removed under this work. Cleanup is limited to living, recreational, and working areas of the authorized property unless the State directs otherwise in writing. Metal, burnt vehicles, and appliances go to recyclers when practicable; other non-hazardous debris generally goes to the Tok landfill. How to submit Email the signed packet and insurance attachments to DHSEM.PublicAssistance@Alaska.gov. Use the subject line Private Property Debris Removal. When emailing, DHS&EM requests that the file be named, if possible, as PPDR.LastName.FirstInitial (example: PPDR.Smith.J). You may also deliver the completed packet to a DHS&EM Debris Monitor or to the debris-removal contractor. If the packet is delivered to the Debris Monitor or the contractor, work may not begin until the Debris Monitor certifies the form complete and authorizes work. Questions about eligibility, insurance, or program decisions should be directed to DHS&EM, not the debris-removal contractor. For assistance, call the DHS&EM Public Assistance Hotline at (907) 428-7097. full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE May 21, 2021 Contact: Jeremy Zidek (907) 441-2337 Multiagency task force deploys to Buckland following Gov. Dunleavy’s Disaster Declaration Task force to coordinate state response and conduct a Preliminary Damage Assessment JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – A task force, deployed by the State Emergency Operations Center, comprised of emergency management specialists, State Department of Environmental Conservation, Red Cross of Alaska, and the North West Arctic Borough (NWAB) are in Buckland today to coordinate the state’s response and conduct a Preliminary Damage Assessment (PDA) after Governor Mike Dunleavy issued a disaster declaration on May 19. The disaster declaration was made after an ice jam on the Buckland River caused major flooding throughout the community. The task force will meet with Buckland City and Tribal representatives, determine immediate mass care needs, conduct preliminary assessments of damages to homes and infrastructure, evaluate hazardous materials released during the flooding, and begin preparations for delivery of the state Individual Assistance and Public Assistance disaster programs. The Alaska State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management (DHS&EM) plans to open a Disaster Assistance Center in Buckland in early June to help residents with damages to their homes apply for the state’s Individual Assistance program. The state’s Individual Assistance program can help eligible applicants with expenses like temporary housing or damages to essential personal property from a declared disaster. On May 12, an ice jam formed approximately one-quarter mile downriver from the community of Buckland, located within NWAB. The community stood up their Incident Command Team as the water began to rise and took emergency protective measures throughout the flooding. While Buckland was able to respond to the event with local resources, the NWAB and the state were ready to support if needed. “Buckland’s response to this event was tremendous. It was a textbook example of how a small community, and a regional borough government, should respond to a local disaster event,” said Bryan Fisher, acting director of the DHS&EM. “Their swift response, and the abundance of response information, made our recommendation that the Governor declare a disaster straight forward.” ###

Storm survivors who are seeking NCS should call the NCS Assistance Line at 907-759-6927. “We are grateful to the Red Cross, Salvation Army Alaska Division, Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, the City of Anchorage, the University of Alaska and the numerous other organizations and volunteers who have supported the survivors and made the transition as smooth as possible,” said Bryan Fisher, Director of the Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. “This transition will help families as they continue to put their lives back together. We will continue to work with organizations providing services to storm survivors to ensure their needs are met.” Services for displaced families will continue to be offered in NCS and other locations. In coordination with the Calista Corporation, a Disaster Assistance Center (DAC) will be open through Friday Oct. 31 from 10am – 5pm. It is located at 5015 Business Park Blvd., Suite 1300, Anchorage, AK 99503. The DACs will help with registering for Individual Assistance services from both FEMA and the state. full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 31, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907- 428-7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov SEOC Update: 2025 October West Coast Storm – Disaster Update JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska — A Major Disaster Declaration has been signed by President Trump in response to a state-declared disaster, for the 2025 October West Coast Storms, including Typhoon Halong and related storms. The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) is coordinating with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to transition from a state-led response to a joint, long-term recovery operation through a Unified Command. The primary focus is life sustainment and stabilization for the impacted area. Recovery is a priority for the impacted areas, and recovery operations continue with an emphasis on restoring critical infrastructure and services – including water, power, and communications, and emergency home and boardwalk repairs. Coordination between federal, state, local and tribal partners is continuing to provide critical supplies to impacted communities and address community needs as they are reported. As of this afternoon, 1,177 applications for state Individual Assistance (IA) have been received. FEMA has received 321 IA applications to date. State IA and FEMA IA are coordinating to share information and encourage applicants register for each program All individuals residing in congregate shelters in Anchorage and Bethel have transitioned to non-congregate sheltering, some shelters will remain in standby status for the coming days to accept potential evacuees. Some survivors may be sheltering with neighbors, family, or friends; it is crucial that those who are affected by the recent storms register for both state and federal IA programs and other forms of assistance. State of Alaska Individual Assistance (IA) – Deadline is December 9, 2025 To register for State of Alaska Individual Assistance: Call 1-844-445-7131, Monday – Friday, 8 a.m. – 4 p.m. Or apply online https://ready.alaska.gov/Recovery/IA FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) – Deadline is December 22, 2025 To register for FEMA Individual Assistance: Call 1-866-342-1699, Monday – Sunday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m. Or apply online at https://disasterassistance.gov 2 Red Cross Assistance To Register for assistance through the American Red Cross: Call 1-800-RED-CROSS Non-Congregate Sheltering (NCS) To register for long-term, temporary, housing in the Non-Congregate Shelter Program: Call 907-759-6927, Monday – Friday 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Congregate shelters remain open in Anchorage and Bethel in standby status, ready to provide immediate sheltering needs if presented. A total of 92 households, consisting of 379 individuals, have transitioned from congregate to non-congregate sheltering in Anchorage. Plans for longer-term temporary housing are currently in development. Alaska 211 can connect individuals with available local resources that best fit their needs. Call 2-1-1 or 1-800-478-2221. Email: alaska211@ak.org or visit www.Alaska211.org. Native Alaskan language interpretation services are available. Reunification of pets is ongoing. Team Rubicon is coordinating the collection of new items only for donations. To donate new items, bring them to Team Rubicon at the Chugach Electric Warehouse located at 1120 East 1st Avenue, Anchorage, AK, daily from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. A list of resources related to the disaster is available at ready.alaska.gov, under Top News. full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE November 21, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907-428- 7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov West Coast Storm Operations Transitions from Response to Recovery JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska — The 2025 October West Coast Storms response effort is entering a transition to recovery. The Alaska Organized Militia (AKOM), the Alaska Division of Forestry & Fire Prevention, and Team Rubicon drawing down of emergency repair operations in the villages have begun. This drawdown is anticipated to be completed between Nov. 22 – 26. Alaska Army National Guard aircraft and aircrew will remain in Bethel to provide continued support to recovery efforts at the request of the State Emergency Operations Center. Repair operations will continue in the impacted areas, with an emphasis on restoring critical infrastructure and services. While some organizations are transitioning out of the area, coordination between federal, state, local and tribal partners is continuing to address community needs and provide critical support. “Some aspects of the recovery operation might look different, but the support for impacted individuals and communities will continue, ” said Director Bryan Fisher of the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. “The work to get emergency repair personnel, supplies, and equipment to communities and repair homes has been nothing short of amazing. The Alaska Organized Militia, Division of Forestry and Fire Protection, and Team Rubicon have accomplished so much in a short time. I want to thank them for their dedications and compassion they brough to this mission” Following the transition date of Nov. 22, the Association of Village Council Presidents (AVCP), the Association of Village Council Presidents Regional Housing Authority (AVCP RHA), Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities and community organizations may continue to work in the villages as weather allows. “As winter conditions become more challenging, progress to repair critical infrastructure may continue, ” said Fisher. “The focus for survivors is to return those who can return home back to their community, providing temporary housing for those who cannot return, and developing plans for a spring rebuilding effort. ” As ﬁnancial assistance begins to ﬂow to State and FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) applicants it is essential that beneﬁts are not duplicated. Neither state or FEMA IA allows for ﬁnancial assistance for home repairs to be paid when emergency repair response workers are making the same repairs or providing the same materials. When beneﬁts are duplicated state and FEMA IA programs must seek repayment from applicants or disqualify them from future eligibility. Minimizing the duplication of beneﬁts will enable survivors to take full advantage of long-term recovery options being developed now and throughout the winter. Survivors from the impacted areas can continue to register for disaster assistance through the state's Individual Assistance program, FEMA’s Individual Assistance, and the Small Business Administration. Registration info. Disaster survivors are encouraged to visit the State of Alaska Division of Homeland Security website at www.Ready.Alaska.Gov for disaster response updates, individual assistance registrations, and other 2025 West Coast Storm Recovery information. The 2025 West Coast Storm Recovery Facebook Group is also a source of information for survivors. ### Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907-428- 7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov

full_text: PRESS RELEASE August 14, 2025 By Jeremy Zidek Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: Jeremy Zidek, 907-428-7077 Governor Dunleavy Declares State Disaster for Juneau Flood Threat, Activates Public and Individual Assistance Funding JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska - In response to the imminent threat of catastrophic flooding from a glacier lake outburst flood (GLOF) originating from Suicide Basin, a side basin of the Mendenhall Glacier, Governor Mike Dunleavy issued a State Disaster Declaration on August 9, 2025. This declaration activates State of Alaska Public Assistance, Individual Assistance, and Temporary Housing programs to support the City and Borough of Juneau and its residents. The disaster declaration also allows for certain permitting requirements to be waived, expediting emergency protective work and recovery efforts. Assistance Programs Activated by the Declaration: • Public Assistance Program: This program provides grants to local jurisdictions, tribal entities, and eligible non-profits to repair critical infrastructure damaged by the disaster. The grants reimburse applicants for eligible repairs to restore infrastructure to its pre-disaster condition and cover the costs of emergency protective measures taken before and during the response. • Individual Assistance (IA) Program: IA helps individuals and families with expenses related to their primary homes, including repairs, replacement of critical items, repair or replacement of damaged primary transportation, and disaster- related medical costs. Applicants must first complete their insurance claims and accept other forms of assistance to be eligible for state IA. • Temporary Housing (TH) Program: This program assists disaster survivors who are unable to return to their homes by providing funding for longer-term housing. TH can provide support for homeowners for up to 18 months and renters for up to three months while their homes are being repaired or alternative housing is secured. Resident Registration Information: Registration for the Individual Assistance and Temporary Housing programs will be available to Juneau residents starting August 14, 2025 from 9 am to 4 pm. The Deadline to apply is October 13,2025 To register for state Individual Assistance, call 844-445-7131. Register online at Ready.Alaska.Gov. To expedite the process, have proof of ownership and insurance documents ready to submit. A list of damaged items and photographs will be needed. full_text: #mvaweb FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE February 26, 2021 Media contact: Jeremy Zidek, 907-441-2337 Multiagency response and recovery efforts continue after Tuluksak water plant fire JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – Response and recovery efforts continue this week in Tuluksak after the community’s water plant was destroyed in a fire last month. Personnel from the Alaska Department of Military and Veterans Affairs visited Tuluksak Monday and Tuesday. The department’s tribal liaison and an emergency management specialist met with local leaders to tour the temporary water treatment facilities, assess the amount of available potable water, and discuss the community’s plans for short- and long-term solutions. “Much work has been done to ensure Alaskans in Tuluksak have sufficient potable water supplies,” said DMVA’s Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management director, Paul Nelson. “We have a long way to go before Tuluksak will have a long-term solution to the water issues they are experiencing, but temporary options remain available, and work to improve the situation continues.” Donated drinking water has been distributed within the community since the week of the fire and continues to be shipped in regularly, including an additional 10 pallets this week. More than 500 gallons of donated water are currently stored in the Tuluksak Native Council office. The Kuskokwim ice road to Bethel and Akiak is being maintained and, weather permitting, the communities are able to resupply Tuluksak with potable water, which may be transported with several large water tanks that were donated to the village. The Yukon Kuskokwim Health Corporation established a temporary non-potable water supply with a 1,600- gallon holding tank capable of producing 12 gallons of water per minute. With additional filters, the water may be able to qualify as a potable water source for the community. The Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation determined that water from the Tuluksak and Kuskokwim Rivers may be used as a source of drinking and cleaning water after it has been boiled. Water was supplied to the school to charge the sprinkler system, and plans are now underway to repair several leaks that were discovered, which should allow the school to reopen within two weeks. A multi-agency group continues to discuss long-term funding solutions. Indian Health Service, Bureau of Indian Affairs, U.S. Housing and Urban Development, and State of Alaska funds may be utilized to address rebuilding efforts. “The State of Alaska is committed to working with the community, regional partners, non-government organizations, and the private sector to see them through this disaster,” said Nelson. ###

A Request for Federal Assistance is under consideration by President Trump. The SEOC remains at Level 4 – Major Incident Response. Disaster Assistance Centers (DAC) are planned for Anchorage and Bethel. These DACs will assist with and collect applications for state Individual Assistance. More information will be provided once locations are finalized. As of this afternoon, 840 applications for state Individual Assistance have been received. Survivors in designated disaster areas may register for the State of Alaska’s Individual Assistance program: • Online: https://ready.alaska.gov/ia • By phone: 1-844-445-7131 The program provides financial assistance for damages to primary residences, vehicles, essential personal property, and medical, funeral, or dental needs directly resulting from the declared disaster. Individuals who are impacted by the disaster and are not staying at either shelter in Anchorage are encouraged to register for the state’s Individual Assistance program to begin registration for long-term housing assistance. The Alaska Department of Motor Vehicles in cooperation with the Alaska Department of Health will have a booth at the two shelters in Anchorage to provide access to their services: Alaska Airlines Center Tuesday, October 21, 2025 from 9 am to 5 pm Friday, October 24, 2025 from 12 pm to 5 pm Egan Center Thursday, October 23, 2025 from 9 am to 5 pm 2 Friday, October 24, 2025 from 9 am to 5 pm Congregate shelters remain open in Anchorage and Bethel. Additional survivors may be sheltering with neighbors, family, or friends in multiple communities. Last night, a total of 338 individuals were reported sheltering: Egan Center – 178, Alaska Airlines Center – 160. The SEOC is working to identify the next steps forward to secure safe, warm housing for the winter. "The state and Alaska Housing Finance Corporation is leading the West Coast Storm Housing Task Force. The goal is to work with all partners to get evacuees out of group shelters and into better accommodations, in some cases longer-term temporary housing," said Governor Mike Dunleavy. The SEOC is continuing to coordinate with other state, local, and tribal agencies to deliver supplies and needed personnel to the impacted communities; addressing needs as they are presented. full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE November 4, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907- 428-7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov SEOC Update: 2025 October West Coast Storm – Disaster Update JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska — A Major Disaster Declaration has been signed by President Trump in response to a state-declared disaster, for the 2025 October West Coast Storms, including Typhoon Halong and related storms. The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) is coordinating with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to transition from a state-led response to a joint, long-term recovery operation through a Unified Command. The primary focus is life sustainment and stabilization for the impacted area. Recovery is a priority for the impacted areas, and recovery operations continue with an emphasis on restoring critical infrastructure and services – including water, power, and communications, and emergency home and boardwalk repairs. Coordination between federal, state, local and tribal partners is continuing to provide critical supplies to impacted communities and address community needs as they are reported. As of this afternoon, 1,305 applications for state Individual Assistance (IA) have been received. FEMA has received 577 IA applications to date. State IA and FEMA IA are coordinating to share information and encourage applicants to register for each program. All individuals residing in congregate shelters in Anchorage and Bethel have transitioned to non-congregate sheltering, some shelters will remain in standby status for the coming days to accept potential evacuees. The Egan Civic and Convention Center shelter will close today, marking its final day of operations. Beginning November 5, shelter services will transition to the Spenard Community Recreation Center, located at 2020 W 48th Ave, Anchorage, AK 99517. The facility will be open daily from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. The Spenard Community Recreation Center will provide temporary shelter for individuals displaced by the 2025 October West Coast Storm and will serve as a short- term pass-through location as survivors move into the non-congregate sheltering program. 2 Some survivors may be sheltering with neighbors, family, or friends; it is crucial that those who are affected by the recent storms register for both state and federal IA programs and other forms of assistance. State of Alaska Individual Assistance (IA) – Deadline is December 9, 2025 To register for State of Alaska Individual Assistance: Call 1-844-445-7131, Monday – Friday, 8 a.m. – 4 p.m. Or apply online https://ready.alaska.gov/Recovery/IA FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) – Deadline is December 22, 2025 To register for FEMA Individual Assistance: Call 1-866-342-1699, Monday – Sunday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m. Or apply online at https://disasterassistance.gov Red Cross Assistance To register for assistance through the American Red Cross: Call 1-800-RED-CROSS Non-Congregate Sheltering (NCS) To register for long-term, temporary, housing in the Non-Congregate Shelter Program: Call 907-759-6927, Monday – Friday 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Congregate shelters remain open in Anchorage and Bethel in standby status, ready to provide immediate sheltering needs if presented. A total of 567 individuals have transitioned from congregate to non-congregate sheltering in Anchorage. Plans for longer-term temporary housing are currently in development. Anchorage Disaster Assistance Center (DAC) A DAC will be operating at the Calista Corporation Building located at 1400 W. Benson Blvd, Suite 110, Anchorage, AK. The DAC will be open November 3 – 14, 2025, Monday – Friday 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. Alaska 211 can connect individuals with available local resources that best fit their needs. Call 2-1-1 or 1-800-478-2221. Email: alaska211@ak.org or visit www.Alaska211.org. Native Alaskan language interpretation services are available. Reunification of pets is ongoing. Evacuees can contact the following for assistance: Alaska Pet Help Line: 907-615-8904, Bethel Friends of Canines: 907-707-7010, Mat-Su Animal Shelter: 907-746-5500 or 907-761-7501, or the Anchorage Shelter: 907-343- 8138. The Alaska Native Medical Center and The Alaska Native Heritage Center are continuing to accept donations of subsistence-based traditional foods. Team Rubicon is coordinating the collection of new items only for donations. To donate new items, bring them to Team Rubicon at the Chugach Electric Warehouse located at 1120 East 1st Avenue, Anchorage, AK, daily from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Team Rubicon is asking that donors send their donations to the warehouse, not hand deliver them. They also recommend that people and organizations wanting to contribute to the long-term recovery of survivors donate monetarily to reputable organizations such as Team 3 Rubicon https://teamrubiconusa.org/ or the The Alaska Community Foundation https://alaskacf.org/. A list of resources related to the disaster is available at ready.alaska.gov, under Top News. Survivors are also encouraged to visit Alaska Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster (VOAD) for additional resources https://www.akvoad.org/. All donations, events, and services available for survivors of the 2025 October West Coast Storm should be directed to storm2025@ready.alaska.gov. Interagency Partner Operations Alaska Organized Militia (AKOM): There are 63 AKOM members activated on State Active Duty with additional authorization as needed for disaster response. AKOM is assisting the Division of Forestry & Fire Protection with winterization, debris removal, muck-outs and supporting cargo flights. American Red Cross: The Red Cross continues to support the recovery by providing assistance with IA registrations, non-congregate housing, and Red Cross Individual Assistance. Association of Village Council Presidents (AVCP): AVCP is working to develop a plan for the transition to long-term recovery, managed by AVCP. There are still many survivors from the affected villages with unidentified needs. Team Rubicon encourages anyone in the Y-K Delta with remaining needs due to the storm to email familyrequest@avcp.org. Team Rubicon is working alongside the AVCP. This email will help volunteers in Bethel fulfill these requests and AVCP get the items needed to those who need them. The Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC): DEC is working closely with communities, local governments, tribal and regional organizations, and state and federal partners to support recovery efforts in Western Alaska. This live website provides daily updates on the status of drinking water, wastewater, solid waste, and environmental conditions in affected communities: https://dec.alaska.gov/commish/west-coast-alaska-storm-response-2025/ U.S. Postal Service (USPS): Mail delivery continues to be available at the USPS Egan Center Mail Unit for residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok. Pickup is available daily between 1:00 p.m. and 4 p.m. daily. Individuals are encouraged by USPS to complete a Change of Address (COA) request, to prevent an interruption in mail delivery. COA forms are available in person at any post office or online at https://www.usps.com. For additional assistance, contact USPS Alaska Customer Relations at 907-564-2828. ### Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907- 428-7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov

full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 16, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: Public Information Officer Jeremy Zidek 907-441-2337, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov SEOC Update: 2025 October West Coast Storm – Situation Update JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska — The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) activation level remains at level 4 – Major Incident Response, Alaska SEOC’s highest level. The SEOC’s top priority has shifted from life safety to life sustainment and shelter operations. Alaska State Troopers are requesting that anyone who knows of additional people who are unaccounted for, please contact the Alaska State Troopers at 907-451-5100. The Troopers will continue to coordinate with the local community to continue recovery efforts for the two missing individuals. The SEOC, in cooperation with Alaska National Guard and multiple state, local, and volunteer agencies, initiated the first airlift evacuations of 282 residents sheltering in Bethel on Wednesday, October 15 to an Anchorage shelter. Today, two additional air evacuation transports from Bethel to Anchorage were conducted. Evacuation from each community is an individual survivor decision and SEOC coordinates with each local community’s leadership and regional tribal organizations in any evacuation. The goal is to move people who cannot return home to a place that is safe and warm with basic human needs. The American Red Cross is coordinating the sheltering and food service response. Additional support is being provided by the Municipality of Anchorage, Department of Health, University of Alaska, Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection, Salvation Army, and other volunteer and private-sector organizations. Many Alaskans, people from the lower-48 states, and companies have donated services to help Alaskan disaster survivors. The American Red Cross has additional staff in Anchorage and Bethel assisting with sheltering, wrap around support, and other mass care needs. The World Central Kitchen has arrived and is coordinating feeding of the survivors in shelters. The Salvation Army is supporting mass care and working to coordinate donation management and sheltering needs. 2 For those wishing to make donations, cash donations are preferred and are being accepted through the Alaska Community Foundation’s Western Alaska Disaster Relief Fund. Additional information can be found at: https://alaskacf.org. The SEOC is currently staffed with more than 70 representatives from across all state agencies, non-governmental and community organizations, tribal organizations, and federal partners coordinating the response and recovery efforts for the 2025 West Coast Storms. There are 103 Alaska National Guard servicemembers activated on State Active Duty with an additional 20 servicemembers expected today for disaster response missions. The SEOC is requesting calls for non-critical evacuations be made to the Yukon Kuskokwim Health Corporation. For life-threatening emergency rescues, please contact the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center at 907-551-7230. The State of Alaska is receiving support from multiple states through the Emergency Management Assistance Compact (EMAC). Currently engaged in the response are personnel from Colorado, Virginia, South Carolina, Virginia, Arkansas, and Texas. More EMAC resources are enroute to Alaska. As of this morning, DHS&EM has received 306 applications for Individual Assistance. State of Alaska Individual Assistance Disaster survivors in the designated disaster area can register for the state's Individual Assistance program by visiting the DHS&EM registration webpage at https://ready.alaska.gov/ia. Telephone registration is available at 1-844-445-7131. The State's Individual Assistance (IA) program is designed to provide financial assistance to individuals or families for damage to a primary residence, primary mode of transportation, essential personal property, and medical/funeral/dental needs created as a direct result of a declared disaster. The SEOC understands that one of the most heartbreaking decisions people had to make during this disaster was leaving their pets behind. For many, animals are beloved members of the family, and being forced to evacuate without them adds another layer of stress and grief to an already overwhelming situation. Safety and survival often require impossible choices in moments like these, and we want every pet owner to know that their love and concern for their animals has not gone unnoticed. At this time evacuation of people is the priority. The state’s Mass Care Task Force and our partner agencies, including the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation State Veterinarian’s Office, are actively working to coordinate rescue efforts for stranded and displaced animals. Every effort is being made to reunite families with their animals safely and as quickly as possible. Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta 3 Damage assessments for the communities are continuing to be coordinated with Department of Transportation and Public Facilities DOT&PF, Alaska Association of Village Council Presidents, and Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium. Bethel – Yesterday, SEOC has a Response Branch in place coordinating state disaster response with personnel from the SEOC and Division of Forestry and Fire Protection. 264 people were airlifted from Bethel to Anchorage yesterday. 492 people evacuated from Kwigillingok and Kipnuk. At the time of this report, two additional airlifts of survivors were underway to move survivors to shelters in Anchorage. Kipnuk – AEA reports 75% or more of the distribution is heavily damage and will take longer to repair. Kwigillingok – Staff are completing evacuation operations in Kwig and beginning evacuations in neighboring villages today. Alaska Energy Authority reports partial power restored in community. Quinhagak – A Department of Environmental Conservation Remote Maintenance Worker is on site working to make repairs to the water infrastructure and assess further damage. Water supplies are impacted. Nightmute –The power is on with multiple homes with damage. Norton Sound/Nome Impacts to the Norton Sound and Nome area were not severe from the storm or Typhoon Halong. Power was restored to east side of Elim on October 15th and GCI communication are restored. Northwest Arctic Borough/Kotzebue The SEOC has a Branch Director in Kotzebue to assist the Northwest Arctic Borough (NWAB), Kivalina, and the City of Kotzebue with disaster response and recovery. Kotzebue – The local Alaska Commercial grocery store received a shipment of perishable goods. 17 Alaska Organized Militia servicemembers and 9 NWAB/VPSO personnel remain deployed. 150 homes and buildings have initial damage assessments complete. Kivalina – No one in shelters overnight. ### Media Contact: Public Information Officer Jeremy Zidek 907-441-2337, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov

full_text: PRESS RELEASE August 12, 2026 By Jeremy Zidek Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: Jeremy Zidek, 907-428-7077 Governor Dunleavy Issues Disaster Declaration in Response to Imminent Glacial Flood Threat in Juneau JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska — Governor Mike Dunleavy has issued a State Disaster Declaration in response to an imminent threat of catastrophic flooding caused by a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) originating from Suicide Basin, a side basin of the Mendenhall Glacier. The declaration follows formal requests for assistance submitted by the City and Borough of Juneau (CBJ) and the Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska. Glacial lake outburst floods have become a recurring issue in the region, triggering state and federal disaster recovery responses in both 2023 and 2024. In 2025, the State of Alaska issued a preemptive disaster declaration when an outburst became imminent. Thanks to a temporary flood barrier constructed by CBJ and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), record-high water levels during the 2025 event were contained, preventing severe inundation in residential neighborhoods. This latest declaration activates the State of Alaska Public Assistance disaster recovery program. Additionally, the declaration allows the state to temporarily waive certain administrative regulations that could otherwise impede immediate prevention or mitigation efforts, such as clearing waterway debris that threatens flood-control barriers. Hydrologic monitoring conducted by the National Weather Service (NWS) confirms that water has begun releasing from Suicide Basin, causing water levels on the Mendenhall River to rise. "CBJ, the Tlingit and Haida Tribe, USACE, and local partner agencies have done a remarkable job constructing flood defenses, coordinating response efforts, and preparing Mendenhall Valley residents," said Bryan Fisher, Director of the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. "Their proactive efforts serve as a model for community safety and emergency preparedness." The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) has elevated its operational state to actively support local and tribal management efforts. This includes facilitating interagency coordination, streamlining emergency permits, managing public communications, and positioning response assets. The SEOC will deploy three emergency management personnel to Juneau to monitor conditions on the ground during the flood window. Residents in affected areas are urged to stay informed and prepare for potential flooding. Official updates, evacuation guidance, and emergency resources can be accessed at www.juneauflood.com. ### Media Contact: Jeremy Zidek Public Information Officer Alaska Division of Homeland Security & Emergency Management jeremy.zidek@alaska.gov | (907) 428-7083

full_text: For Immediate Release January 4, 2022 Contact: Jeremy Zidek (907) 441-2337 Press Release: State of Alaska Individual Assistance provides disaster recovery grants to those impacted by 2021-2022 Alaska Winter Storm Individuals and families can now apply for state disaster recovery grants JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska — Governor Mike Dunleavy declared the 2021-2022 Alaska Winter Storm a State Disaster on January 3, 2022, in response to numerous impacts from extreme cold weather, high winds, freezing rain, and heavy snowfall. These conditions interrupted power and water distribution, damaged public buildings and homes, restricted travel, and required communities to establish shelter locations for displaced residents. The Jan. 3 declaration activates the state’s Individual Assistance (IA) program which is designed to help individuals and families with damages and/or expenses related to the disaster event. Residents in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, Denali Borough, Fairbanks North Star Borough including Nenana, Delta/Greely Regional Education Attendance Area, and the Copper River Regional Education Attendance Area, may be eligible for disaster recovery grants for damages to their primary residences that occurred during the 2021-2022 Alaska Winter Storms. Disaster survivors can register for the State Individual Assistance program by visiting the State of Alaska’s Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management webpage at Ready.Alaska.Gov Online Registration Begins January 4th, 2022 at Ready.Alaska.Gov Registration Deadline March 4, 2022 If you have any questions or issues applying online, please call 1-855-445-7131(Disaster Assistance Hotline) The State of Alaska IA program has three parts; Temporary Housing grants; Housing Assistance grants; Other Needs Assistance grants. Temporary Housing can provide funds to secure lodging while applicants pursue permanent housing solutions. Financial assistance may be available for up to 18 months for owners and three months for renters. Housing Assistance grants can provide funds for damages to primary residences not covered by insurance. The residence must be owner-occupied at the time of the event. The IA program does not help with secondary homes, recreational properties or homes lived in fewer than six months a year. Damages must be serious and negatively impact the essential living spaces in the home, and damages must be from the declared event. Other Needs Assistance can provide funds for losses to essential personal property not covered by insurance such as clothing, appliances and furniture. Also, recovery costs such as clean up and some storage expenses. It may also help with disaster-caused medical/funeral expenses not covered by insurance. Based on damages and eligibility, the maximum grant amount an applicant can receive through Housing Assistance is $18,950, and separately, an additional $18,950 for Other Needs Assistance. Temporary Housing is calculated separately based on family size and local rates of stay. The State of Alaska is working with federal partners to identify programs that may become available to disaster survivors. If activated, federal disaster assistance must be pursued before a State IA award. More IA information can be found at www.ready.alaska.gov/Recovery/IndividualAssistance ###

full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE November 22, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: Public Information Officer Jeremy Zidek 907-441-2337, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov Financial Donations Encouraged for Organizations Supporting Alaskans Affected by the 2025 West Coast Storms JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska - As the management of the response to the October 2025 West Coast Storms evolves from the emergency to recovery phase, members of the public are encouraged to support the survivors by giving financial donations to nonprofit organizations that are assisting affected individuals and families. Many agencies that are assisting in the response to the catastrophic storms, which destroyed many West Coast homes and displaced about 2,000 Alaskans, would now prefer financial donations as many of the initial urgent material needs have been met and centers that collect donations are either full or closing for the winter. Financial Donations Monetary donations offer organizations the most flexibility in obtaining the most-needed resources. Organizations typically prefer cash donations because they allow those helping survivors to: ● Purchase survivor-specific food, water, medicine, and equipment from secure and familiar supply chains. ● Conserve resources. Money is always necessary and cheap to send, but the cost of shipping material supplies can be expensive. ● Remember, material supplies such as used clothing, miscellaneous household items, and mixed or perishable food require helping agencies to redirect volunteer labor away from providing direct one-on-one assistance to sort, package, transport, warehouse, and distribute items that may not meet the needs of disaster survivors. Avoiding Scams Unfortunately, scam operations often appear during times of crisis, preying on the generosity of well-intentioned donors. Before donating, you can use sites like Charity Navigator and Give.org to check for an organization’s ratings, financial health, and transparency. Choose reputable disaster relief organizations with a proven track record, such as: ● American Red Cross ● Food Bank of Alaska ● Team Rubicon ● The Salvation Army ● World Central Kitchen ● Faith-based organizations known for disaster response efforts such as Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster (Alaska VOAD) Several local community organizations and regional partners have come together to establish the Western Alaska Disaster Relief Fund through the Alaska Community Foundation. Donate to the fund through the Alaska Community Foundation website at https://alaskacf.org. Resource Links ● FEMA Donation Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6b1-tkV77s ### Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907- 428- 7142, Jeremy.Zidek@alaska.gov

full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE December 11, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907- 428-7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov State Individual Assistance available for Storm Survivors until Jan. 8 State disaster recovery programs active in areas not named in federal declaration JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska — The Alaska Division of Homeland Security & Emergency Management (DHS&EM) is accepting applications for State Individual Assistance (IA) from survivors who have experienced damages or emergency expenses from the severe storms, flooding, and remnants of Typhoon Halong that occurred Oct. 8 – 13, 2025.This State of Alaska disaster recovery assistance is available in areas not named in the federal disaster declaration. “The extension to the Individual Assistance deadline has allowed us to utilize the state programs to the fullest extent possible and provide an opportunity for Alaskans who are impacted by the disaster to register for financial assistance,” said Bryan Fisher, Director for the Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. “Alaska is one of the only states in the nation with a state IA program.” The federally declared disaster area includes the Northwest Arctic Borough, Lower Yukon Regional Education Attendance Area (REAA) and Lower Kuskokwim REAA. full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE July 30, 2021 By Public Information Officer Jeremy Zidek SOA Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: Jeremy Zidek, (907) 441-2337, jeremy.zidek@alaska.gov DHS&EM to deploy personnel to conduct post-earthquake preliminary damage assessment JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska — Alaska’s Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management (DHS&EM) will deploy a team to conduct a damage assessment in communities impacted by the July 28 Chignik Earthquake. The team will depart as soon as weather, COVID testing requirements, and aircraft availability allow. The team will visit several impacted communities. DHS&EM will send a team of emergency management specialists to the most severely affected communities. At 10:16 p.m. on July 28, the National Tsunami Warning Center in Palmer, Alaska recorded a magnitude (M)8.2 earthquake 60 miles south of Chignik. The magnitude and location of the earthquake triggered a tsunami warning for an approximately 600-mile-long coastline from Nikolski to the Kenai Peninsula. Based upon the warning, multiple communities within the warning area evacuated to higher ground. “This was the largest earthquake Alaska has experienced in more than 50 years. We Alaskans are extremely fortunate a large tsunami wave was not generated, and that no one was severely injured by the shaking,” said DHS&EM Director Bryan Fisher. “While we cannot predict earthquakes or tsunamis, we can have plans in place to react to these events. Throughout the tsunami warning and advisory area communities responded and quickly evacuated their residents. Our alert system worked, and people were able to get to safety before the estimated wave arrival time. The USGS Shake Map produced for the earthquake showed the highest seismic shaking intensities in Cold Bay, Sand Point, Perryville and Chignik areas of the Alaska Peninsula. The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) conducted a full communication check with all communities in the warned areas within one hour of the tsunami warning. The SEOC is in contact with State of Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities, the Lake and Peninsula Borough, the Aleutians East Borough, and several other communities to assess earthquake damage, including residential and public facility damages. The SEOC received reports of minor damages to mostly residential or recreational structures in a few communities, but a complete assessment is ongoing. ###

The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) is coordinating with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to transition from a state-led response to a joint, long-term recovery operation through a Unified Command. The primary focus is life sustainment and stabilization for the impacted area. Recovery is a priority for the impacted areas, and recovery operations continue with an emphasis on restoring critical infrastructure and services – including water, power, and communications, and emergency home and boardwalk repairs. Coordination between federal, state, local and tribal partners is continuing to provide critical supplies to impacted communities and address community needs as they are reported. As of this afternoon, 1,280 applications for state Individual Assistance (IA) have been received. FEMA has received 518 IA applications to date. State IA and FEMA IA are coordinating to share information and encourage applicants to register for each program. All individuals residing in congregate shelters in Anchorage and Bethel have transitioned to non-congregate sheltering, some shelters will remain in standby status for the coming days to accept potential evacuees. Some survivors may be sheltering with neighbors, family, or friends; it is crucial that those who are affected by the recent storms register for both state and federal IA programs and other forms of assistance. full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE March 24, 2021 Contact: Jeremy Zidek (907) 441-2337 March 27 is the anniversary of the 1964 Good Friday Earthquake JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – The 1964 Good Friday Earthquake was the second largest earthquake ever recorded. On March 27, 1964 a 9.2 magnitude earthquake unleashed nearly five minutes of violent shaking focused in Prince William Sound and felt in a majority of the state. The State of Alaska’s people, communities, and geography were forever changed on that day. Of the 132 people who perished during the 1964 Good Friday Earthquake, 118 lost their lives from tsunamis. During the 1964 Good Friday Earthquake local tsunamis came ashore in some communities before the shaking stopped, while the distance tsunami had lethal effects as far away as Crescent City, California. Governor Mike Dunleavy declared March 21-27 Tsunami Awareness Week. During Tsunami Awareness Week individuals and communities are encouraged to learn about the warning signs of a tsunami, determine if they live in a tsunami vulnerable community, identify evacuation routes to areas outside of the tsunami zone, and to practice earthquake and tsunami safety drills. “In Alaska we have more earthquakes than the rest of the United States combined, but when we talk about earthquakes in Alaska we must also talk about tsunamis. While earthquakes can impact all areas of the state, the additional lethality of tsunamis make it critical we prepare for both simultaneously,” said Paul Nelson, Director of the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. “The Tsunami Ready program, community tsunami sirens, our emergency alert system, and tsunami education within communities combined to make Alaska well prepared for a tsunami response. Several tsunami warnings in the last decade has shown Alaskan communities are ready to take action when needed.” On average Alaska experiences a 7.0 magnitude or greater earthquake every year. The sudden nature of earthquakes does not give an individual or family time to prepare after the event has occurred. Conducting non-structural hazard mitigation, developing a family emergency plan, having emergency supplies, and practicing earthquake safety must be done before the next big earthquake. Earthquake and Tsunami Preparedness Resources: Alaska Earthquake Center https://earthquake.alaska.edu NOAA U.S. Tsunami Warning System www.tsunami.gov The Great Alaska Shakeout www.shakeout.org/alaska 1964 Quake: The Great Alaska Earthquake https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lE2j10xyOgI FEMA - Be Prepared For Tsunami Link ###

full_text: Flooding Preparedness Check List  Talk about the risk - Talk to your family and friends about the risk of flooding and how you can respond. Identify family members who may need assistance before and during a flood and make sure their needs are covered.  Protect your vehicles - Move boats and other vehicles to higher ground. Make sure boats are accessible in case they are needed during the flood.  Make a Plan - Make a family emergency plan so family members know their responsibilities, including children. Make a family communication plan so people know how to communicate. Write down important phone numbers, social media accounts, and other contact information and give a copy to each family member.  Make a Kit - Prepare emergency food, water, medications, fuel, flashlights, batteries, phone chargers, generators, and battery powered radio. Some emergency supplies is better than none.  Gather critical paperwork - Gather critical documents like deeds, titles, birth and marriage certificates, identification, insurance and other documents. Place critical documents in a waterproof bag and in a safe place.  Elevate and Flood Proof - Move things out of reach from rising water. Placing items in water proof containers or plastic bags can prevent damage or loss. Put items on counter tops, shelves, rooftops or anywhere outside the reach of flood waters. Fast rising flood waters may not give you enough time to protect valuables when flooding occurs.  Support Community Preparedness- Talk to your community leaders and know your community flood plan. Identify the community’s shelter and what support is needed to make it ready.  Be pet prepared – Gather pet food and supplies, and identify where pets can be relocated and/or sheltered during the flood event. Do not set pets free as this can become a nuisance to neighbors and other animals.  Keep up to date on conditions – Get your information from trusted sources like community leaders, local media, response organizations, River Watch teams, and the Alaska River Forecast Center. o Visit the Alaska River Forecast Center at weather.gov/aprfc/

full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE September 15, 2021 SOA Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: Jeremy Zidek, (907) 441-2337 Emergency Supply Kit essential to Family and Individual Preparedness September is National Preparedness Month. The Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management is asking individuals and families to take a few easy steps that will help themselves cope with a natural disaster. The DHS&EM recommends each household has enough supplies for two or more weeks. However, assembling any amount of emergency supplies is a good start. Alaskans should not be discouraged if they do not have the time, space, or money to assemble a two-week kit. Good, Better, Best is our campaign to encourage Alaskans to become better prepared for disasters. The campaign focuses on breaking the process of emergency preparedness down to a set of smaller, more attainable goals. This makes the process less overwhelming mentally and financially. “Using a stepped method, we encourage people to become self-sufficient for 3 days (Good) then move up to 7 days (Better) then up to 2 weeks (Best). The goal is to make emergency preparedness to every Alaskan,” said Director Bryan Fisher, DHS&EM. Items an emergency kit should include are: • Food – Self stable easy to prepare food • Water – one gallon, per person, per day • First Aid Kit – with regular medication • Flashlight – avoid open flame for light • Extra Batteries – radio, phone, and light • Radio – NOAA Weather Alerts • Personal Hygiene Items – clean is good • Cash – electronic banking unavailable • Indoor Safe Heat Source – fuel needed • Warm Clothing – all family members For more information on how to start your preparedness journey go to: Ready.Alaska.Gov ###

The declaration follows a joint local disaster declaration and unified request for assistance submitted by the City and Borough of Juneau and the Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska. This joint action reflects the strong coordination and collaboration between municipal and tribal leadership to protect residents, property, and infrastructure from anticipated impacts. Hydrologic monitoring by the National Weather Service (NWS) and U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) confirms that the volume of water currently impounded in Suicide Basin has reached or exceeded levels observed during prior flood-of-record events. A release is expected at any time. Flooding is likely to affect the Mendenhall River and surrounding neighborhoods in the Mendenhall Valley. This year’s conditions follow two consecutive years of severe flooding. The August 2024 GLOF caused widespread damage to homes, public infrastructure, and utilities, resulting in state and federal disaster declaration. To mitigate the impact of future flooding Juneau, and the Army Corps of Engineers, have installed more than 2 miles of flood control barriers along the Mendenhall River. “By issuing this declaration before the flood occurs, we can position state resources and personnel in advance to support local and tribal governments in their efforts to protect lives, homes, and essential services,” said Governor Dunleavy. “Our goal is to act early to reduce impacts and preserve community safety.” The State Emergency Operations Center has been activated to support local and tribal efforts. These efforts include interagency coordination, emergency permitting, public messaging, and preparations for protective actions and potential response. Residents are urged to stay informed and prepared. Official updates and resources are available at www.juneauflood.com. Emergency preparedness information can be found at www.ready.alaska.gov. ### Media Contact: Jeremy Zidek Public Information Officer Alaska Division of Homeland Security & Emergency Management jeremy.zidek@alaska.gov | (907) 428-7083

full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE March 8, 2021 Contact: Jeremy Zidek (907) 441-2337 Water service restored in Unalakleet after disruption due to frozen system JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – The City of Unalakleet restored water service in their community after issuing a local disaster declaration Feb. 26, in response to extreme cold temperatures and high winds that compromised their water treatment and distribution system. A Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management (DHS&EM), emergency management specialist visited the community last week to meet with community leaders, tour the city’s water treatment and distribution facilities, and identify areas where DHS&EM can help the community implement their current water system update plan. The City of Unalakleet, Norton Sound Health Corporation, Department of Environmental Conservation, DHS&EM, and others are working together to address all water issues. The community’s water treatment plant is online, distributing water to most of the community. Three of the community’s four water distribution circuits are functioning, and work continues to restore the last circuit. A well at the Native Village of Unalakleet’s Elders Assisted Living Facility provided potable water during the interruption of water service, and the community organized water delivery to those who could not gather water for themselves. Several other community wells are also available as a source of potable water. The community’s four-mile-long transmission line is producing water and the one-million-gallon water tank is being filled. Once sufficient water is in the tank, a sample will be sent to the Department of Environmental Conservation in order to determine if the boil water notice can be rescinded. The City of Unalakleet is engaged in a multi-year process to upgrade their water system. This effort is funded through a Village Safe Water Capital Improvement Project. In 2018 and 2019, several wells were drilled, but not connected to the community’s water treatment or distribution system. Efforts are being made to expedite this process. ###

full_text: STATE OF ALASKA Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Private Property Debris Removal Mukluk Fire · Tok, Alaska State Disaster AK-26-332 · August 2026 · Community information flyer This State program lets you authorize DHS&EM and its contractors to enter your property and remove eligible Mukluk Fire debris. It is not a general cleanup of everything on the lot. Only disaster debris and wreckage that may threaten public health, safety, or property can be removed. Signing the packet does not guarantee that debris or vehicles will be taken. 1 AM I ELIGIBLE? • Your property is in Tok or the immediately surrounding area affected by the Mukluk Fire. • Debris on the property is a direct result of the fire. • You are the legal owner, or you have legal authority to grant access and authorize removal. • You complete and sign the Combined Debris Removal Authorization Packet. • Debris is in living, recreational, or working areas of the property (not unused acreage, woodlots, or crop/livestock areas unless DHS&EM authorizes that portion in writing). Insured owners are not excluded. Having a homeowners or vehicle policy does not keep you out of the program. 2 DOES THIS COST ME ANYTHING? • There is no application fee and no charge from the State to turn in the packet. • Authorized debris removal under this program is performed by the State’s contractor. You are not billed by the contractor for eligible work. • If your insurance pays (or later pays) for debris removal or vehicle disposal, you must report it. Those proceeds may reduce or offset public assistance so benefits are not paid twice. • You keep responsibility for items the program does not cover, and for any private contractor you hire on your own. • Work is not guaranteed. Eligibility and what is removed are decided by DHS&EM, not by the debris contractor. 3 HOW DO I APPLY AND SUBMIT THE PACKET? 1. Get the packet. Download the Combined Debris Removal Authorization Packet at ready.alaska.gov/Recovery/IA (Forms section). It is a fillable PDF and is printer-friendly — complete it on a computer or print it and fill it by hand. You can also request it from your assigned State Individual Assistance Officer. Contractors and Debris Monitors may carry blank copies. 2. Fill every section that applies. Print clearly. Write N/A if a line does not apply. Include property address, all owners’ legal names, phone, email, mailing address, and approximate date of loss. Attach extra pages if needed. 3. Disclose insurance. Report whether the property (and any vehicle being released) was insured at the time of the fire: company, policy number, claim status, and amounts received or expected. Attach policy, claim, settlement, or denial papers if you have them. 4. All legal owners must sign. Read the indemnification section. Every legal owner, or a person legally authorized to sign, must print name, sign, date, and provide phone and email. If you are not the owner, state your authority. Do not complete the official-use section. 5. Submit it. Email the signed packet and insurance attachments to DHSEM.PublicAssistance@Alaska.gov. Use the subject line Private Property Debris Removal. You may also give the completed packet to your assigned State Individual Assistance Officer, or hand-deliver it to a DHS&EM Debris Monitor or the debris-removal contractor. AK-26-332 · Mukluk Fire · State of Alaska DHS&EM · AS 26.23.110 Page 1 of 2 · Print on letter paper STATE OF ALASKA Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Private Property Debris Removal Mukluk Fire · Tok, Alaska State Disaster AK-26-332 · August 2026 · Community information flyer 4 WHAT HAPPENS AFTER I TURN IT IN? • No work starts until DHS&EM or the independent Debris Monitor confirms the packet is complete and the property is authorized. Handing a packet to the contractor is not enough by itself. • A site assessment comes first. Hazardous materials are removed separately. Then remaining eligible fire debris is hauled away. • Questions about eligibility, insurance, or program decisions go to DHS&EM — not the debris-removal contractor. WHAT MAY BE REMOVED + Collapsed burned structural debris that has already fallen and become wreckage + Household fire debris in living, recreational, and working areas + Appliances and scrap metal (recycled when practicable) + Burned or damaged vehicles you formally release (they will not be returned) + Hazardous materials identified during the first work phase + Ash and fire debris that can be safely handled and hauled WHAT IS NOT REMOVED - Standing walls, roofs, chimneys, or foundations still attached - Demolition of standing structures or leaners - General cleanup of items not caused by the fire - Unused acreage, woodlots, and crop or livestock areas (unless DHS&EM authorizes in writing) - Valuables, heirlooms, and personal property you want to keep - Vehicles you do not release on the packet BEFORE CREWS ARRIVE • Remove valuables and heirlooms you want to keep. Personal property left in released vehicles may be lost. • Disclose known hazards: underground or fuel tanks, chemicals, asbestos, batteries (including lithium), or other environmental hazards. • Provide reasonable access. Released vehicles may be destroyed, recycled, or disposed of and will not be returned. PLEASE READ — WITHDRAWAL, ACCESS DAMAGE, AND ACCURATE INFORMATION Withdrawing. You may withdraw your authorization before work begins on your property by calling the hotline or emailing DHS&EM. If you withdraw after work has started, you may be responsible for costs already incurred. Driveways and access. Heavy equipment must reach the debris. Driveways, access roads, and similar surfaces may crack, rut, or be marked. That incidental damage is an ordinary part of the work and is not repaired under this program. Tell the truth on the packet. The information you provide must be true and complete. Providing false or misleading information may result in civil or criminal penalties and may stop or reverse assistance. full_text: For Immediate Release January 11, 2022 Contact: Jeremy Zidek (907) 441-2337 Press Release: Alaska National Guard to deploy personnel to assist Yakutat with snow removal The State Emergency Operations Center responds to Yakutat’s emergency request JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska — The City and Borough of Yakutat and Southeast Alaska has received tremendous amounts of snow and rain over the last seven days. The State Emergency Operation Center (SEOC) has been working with communities in the region to identify and address critical life health and safety needs. On Jan. 11, 2022 the City and Borough of Yakutat submitted a Declaration of Local Disaster Emergency to the state, and requested assistance with the community’s ongoing emergency. Given the fact that Yakutat is an isolated community off the road system, and all local available resources have been exhausted, the SEOC requested Alaska National Guard support. The SEOC is also working with state, federal, and non-government partners to address emergency assistance requests identified in the community’s declaration. The Alaska National Guard has been requested by the SEOC to build a team of approximately 20 service members and multiple vehicles to be transported to Yakutat, via military airlift, in order to provide emergency snow removal and building safety assessment to the community. Joint Task Force-Yakutat will be comprised of Guardsman from the Air and Army National Guard and is assigned two four-wheel drive vehicles providing direct support to the City and Borough of Yakutat. Actual numbers of deployed service members, vehicles, equipment, and supplies may be decreased or increased through verbal approval from SEOC to accommodate available personnel or mission requirements. The SEOC has received reports of snow and rain impacts in the region to include; collapsed buildings, communities cancelling schools, a Juneau grocery store closed for multiple days, and numerous private and public buildings leaking due to excessive weight on roof tops. At this time there are no reports of serious injury or deaths. “As Alaskans we are accustomed to severe weather, but this winter has been particularly challenging for many areas of the state,” said Director Bryan Fisher, Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. “The state is standing by to help our local jurisdiction when a natural disaster is greater than their local response capabilities. Together with our non-government partners, we will ensure every community receives the emergency assistance they need.” The SEOC is managed by the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, which falls within the Alaska Department of Military and Veterans Affairs. When local authorities determine that an emergency or disaster has caused more impact or damage than the community is able to support independently, they may request assistance through the SEOC. State emergency managers assist local emergency managers in a coordinated effort to provide the necessary resources, effectively and within a codified process. It is through this process that it may be determined that the National Guard’s assistance is needed, and the state requests specific support through the Alaska National Guard Joint Operations Center and Joint Staff, who expedite and coordinate the effort. Additional, snow and rain are forecasted for the region. In addition, an increased avalanche danger exists in many areas. Residents are encouraged to work with their local governments to address needs. ###

full_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE November 6, 2025 Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management Media Contact: State Emergency Operation Center Public Information News Desk 907- 428-7142, Jeremy.Zidek@Alaska.gov SEOC Update: 2025 October West Coast Storm – Disaster Update JOINT BASE ELMENDORF RICHARDSON, Alaska — A Major Disaster Declaration has been signed by President Trump in response to a state-declared disaster, for the 2025 October West Coast Storms, including Typhoon Halong and related storms. The State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC) is coordinating with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to transition from a state-led response to a joint, long-term recovery operation through a Unified Command. The primary focus is life sustainment and stabilization for the impacted area. Recovery is a priority for the impacted areas, and recovery operations continue with an emphasis on restoring critical infrastructure and services – including water, power, and communications, and emergency home and boardwalk repairs. Coordination between federal, state, local and tribal partners is continuing to provide critical supplies to impacted communities and address community needs as they are reported. As of this afternoon, 1,369 applications for state Individual Assistance (IA) have been received. FEMA has received 677 IA applications to date. State IA and FEMA IA are coordinating to share information and encourage applicants to register for each program. All individuals residing in congregate shelters in Anchorage and Bethel have transitioned to non-congregate sheltering, some shelters will remain in standby status for the coming days to accept potential evacuees. Shelter services have transitioned to the Spenard Community Recreation Center, located at 2020 W 48th Ave, Anchorage, AK 99517. The facility will be open daily from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. The Spenard Community Recreation Center will provide temporary shelter for individuals displaced by the 2025 October West Coast Storm and will serve as a short- term pass-through location as survivors move into the non-congregate sheltering program. A total of 577 individuals have transitioned from congregate to non-congregate sheltering in Anchorage. Plans for longer-term temporary housing are currently in development 2 Some survivors may be sheltering with neighbors, family, or friends; it is crucial that those who are affected by the recent storms register for both state and federal IA programs and other forms of assistance. State of Alaska Individual Assistance (IA) – Deadline is December 9, 2025 To register for State of Alaska Individual Assistance: Call 1-844-445-7131, Monday – Friday, 8 a.m. – 4 p.m. Or apply online https://ready.alaska.gov/Recovery/IA FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) – Deadline is December 22, 2025 To register for FEMA Individual Assistance: Call 1-866-342-1699, Monday – Sunday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m. Or apply online at https://disasterassistance.gov Small Business Administration (SBA) – Deadline is December 22, 2025 SBA offers low interest, long-term disaster loans to homeowners, renters, businesses, and private nonprofits to repair and replace property destroyed by the storms. Call 1-800- 659-2955, Monday – Sunday 6 a.m. – 4 p.m. Or apply online at https://sba.gov/disaster Non-Congregate Sheltering (NCS) To register for long-term, temporary, housing in the Non-Congregate Shelter Program: Call 907-759-6927, Monday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Disaster Assistance Centers (DACs) are now open and providing in-person support for survivors in both Anchorage and Bethel. The DAC will be open November 5 – 14, 2025, Monday – Friday 10:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. and 1:00 p.m. – 4 p.m. Alaska 211 can connect individuals with available local resources that best fit their needs. They also recommend that people and organizations wanting to contribute to the long-term recovery of survivors donate monetarily to reputable organizations such as Team Rubicon https://teamrubiconusa.org/ or the The Alaska Community Foundation https://alaskacf.org/. 3 A list of resources related to the disaster is available at ready.alaska.gov, under Top News. Survivors are also encouraged to visit Alaska Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster (VOAD) for additional resources https://www.akvoad.org/. All donations, events, and services available for survivors of the 2025 October West Coast Storm should be directed to storm2025@ready.alaska.gov. Interagency Partner Operations Alaska Organized Militia (AKOM): There are 45 AKOM members activated on State Active Duty with additional authorization as needed for disaster response. AKOM is assisting the Division of Forestry & Fire Protection with winterization, debris removal, muck-outs and supporting cargo flights.
